newsitem.title: USA: Supposed accomplice still shadows U.S. bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Supposed accomplice still shadows U.S. bombing case.

text.p: Is there a John Doe No. 2?
With Timothy McVeigh sentenced to die for the Oklahoma City bombing and Terry Nichols headed for his own trial, questions persist over whether anyone else could have been involved.
An array of witnesses reported seeing another man at critical moments before the April 19, 1995, bombing. Never found nor identified, the mystery man became known as John Doe No. 2.
"I'm completely satisfied he doesn't exist," Weldon Kennedy, who ran the FBI's Oklahoma City bombing investigation, said.
"You don't know how many tens of thousands of man-hours went into this investigation," he said. "Suffice it to say we covered every possible lead and left no end dangling."

Prompted by a witness who saw a stocky, dark-skinned man in a baseball cap accompany McVeigh as he rented a truck before the bombing, authorities launched a massive manhunt for the second man. The description did not fit Nichols, McVeigh's accused co-conspirator.
Later, authorities concluded that the witness was, in fact, remembering a soldier who rented a truck a day after McVeigh.
But not everyone is so sure.

The likelihood that there was a John Doe No. 2 has shrunk in the two years since the bombing, but his existence is still possible, Gerald Posner, an author who has written about criminal investigations and the bombing, said.

Although some witnesses lost credibility and others changed their stories, he said, "In the end, you are confronted by a handful of witnesses who have no apparent reason for lying and appear credible and can't be explained away."

Some employees at the Kansas truck rental agency still think McVeigh was not alone. A man who delivered Chinese food to his motel room said the man at the door was not McVeigh, and the motel owner thought she heard three voices coming from the room.
Minutes before the blast, an Oklahoma City mechanic claimed, McVeigh and another man in a Ryder truck asked for directions.
Many of those who say they spotted John Doe No. 2 did not testify in the McVeigh trial, as prosecutors pared down the evidence and homed in on the defendant.
Daina Bradley, who did testify, said she saw two men emerge from the truck minutes before the explosion. But earlier she recalled seeing only one man, and her credibility faltered.
Kennedy is certain and Posner almost certain that if John Doe existed, he would have been found by now.
McVeigh had a small circle of friends and used a prepaid telephone card that left a record of everyone he called.
As for the eyewitnesses, Kennedy said: "They honestly believe what they saw. I just happen to believe they're mistaken."
None of McVeigh's former friends who testified against him ever mentioned John Doe's existence.
"The question will always linger," Posner said. "If he doesn't exist, he will still exist in folklore as one of the greatest get-away criminals ever."
Like the assassinations of President John Kennedy and Martin Luther King, Kennedy said, the bombing is sure to spawn plenty of conspiracy theories.
"Of course there are some unanswered questions," he said. "But being intimately familiar with this investigation, I can tell you there is no mysterious person out there."
Keeping the mystery alive has been defence attorney Stephen Jones, who said that if McVeigh were executed, he could never reveal whether others were involved.
"Dead men do not tell tales," he said, noting that the original criminal indictment named McVeigh, Nichols and "others unknown."
Lead prosecutor Joe Hartzler scoffed. "What a tease that is," he said. "We're never going to hear from him."
McVeigh remained silent throughout his trial.
With neither McVeigh nor Nichols giving up any secrets, suspicions persist. A poll in April showed three-quarters of those surveyed think not everyone responsible has been captured.
